title: Containerization: Docker and Docker Compose for Automation Stacks
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Containerization: Docker and Docker Compose for Automation Stacks ##### The 1.9 GB image that took eleven minutes to deploy A team containerized their FastAPI automation service. The Dockerfile started `FROM python:3.11`, copied the whole repository, ran `pip install -r requirements.txt`, and started uvicorn as root. The resulting image was 1.9 GB. Every deploy pushed and pulled that, taking eleven minutes. Worse, changing a single line of application code invalidated the layer cache at the `COPY . .` step, so every build reinstalled all dependencies from scratch — four minutes of CI time per commit. The rewrite — multi-stage build, slim base, dependencies copied before source, non-root user — produced a 180 MB image that rebuilt in 20 seconds when only code changed. Same application, 10× smaller, 12× faster. Container overhead itself is near-negligible compared with running natively (Felter et al.'s IBM comparison established this in 2015). The costs that actually bite are the ones you introduce: bloated images, broken caching, lost data, and stacks that cannot be reproduced. ##### Dockerfile: layers, caching, and size Docker builds images as **layers**, one per instruction, each cached. A changed instruction invalidates that layer and everything after it. The entire craft of Dockerfile authoring follows from that one fact: **order instructions from least to most frequently changing.** ```dockerfile # ---------- Stage 1: build dependencies ---------- FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \ PIP_NO_CACHE_DIR=1 \ PIP_DISABLE_PIP_VERSION_CHECK=1 # Build-only tools live in this stage and never reach the final image RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \ build-essential gcc libpq-dev \ && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* WORKDIR /app # Dependencies FIRST: this layer is cached until requirements change COPY requirements.txt . RUN python -m venv /opt/venv \ && /opt/venv/bin/pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt # ---------- Stage 2: runtime ---------- FROM python:3.12-slim AS runtime ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \ PATH="/opt/venv/bin:$PATH" # Runtime libraries only — no compilers RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \ libpq5 curl \ && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* \ && useradd --create-home --uid 10001 appuser COPY --from=builder /opt/venv /opt/venv WORKDIR /app COPY --chown=appuser:appuser ./src ./src # source LAST: changes most often USER appuser # never run as root EXPOSE 8000 HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --start-period=20s --retries=3 \ CMD curl -fsS http://localhost:8000/healthz || exit 1 CMD ["uvicorn", "src.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000", "--workers", "2"] ``` The four decisions that produced the 10× reduction: **Multi-stage build.** `build-essential` and `gcc` are needed to compile wheels but not to run them. Stage two copies only the finished virtualenv, leaving several hundred megabytes of toolchain behind. **Slim base.** `python:3.12-slim` is roughly 150 MB against `python:3.12`'s ~1 GB. `alpine` is smaller still but uses musl libc, which breaks some binary wheels and can be slower — slim is the pragmatic default. **Dependency layer before source.** The `COPY requirements.txt` / `pip install` pair is cached until requirements change, so a code-only edit rebuilds in seconds. **Non-root user.** A container escape as root is a materially worse incident than one as UID 10001. Use a numeric UID so it works under Kubernetes `runAsNonRoot`. Add a `.dockerignore` — omitting it means `COPY` drags in `.git`, `.venv`, test fixtures and `__pycache__`, silently inflating the image and busting the cache on irrelevant changes: ```text .git .venv __pycache__/ *.pyc tests/ .env *.md ``` ##### Compose: the full stack Compose describes multiple services, their networks, volumes and dependencies in one file — turning "clone the repo and run one command" into a reality. ```yaml x-n8n-shared: &n8n-shared image: docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n:1.80.0 restart: unless-stopped environment: &n8n-env DB_TYPE: postgresdb DB_POSTGRESDB_HOST: postgres DB_POSTGRESDB_DATABASE: n8n DB_POSTGRESDB_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER} DB_POSTGRESDB_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD} EXECUTIONS_MODE: queue QUEUE_BULL_REDIS_HOST: redis N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY: ${N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY} GENERIC_TIMEZONE: Asia/Kolkata TZ: Asia/Kolkata depends_on: postgres: { condition: service_healthy } redis: { condition: service_healthy } networks: [backend] services: postgres: image: postgres:16-alpine restart: unless-stopped environment: POSTGRES_USER: ${POSTGRES_USER} POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD} POSTGRES_DB: n8n volumes: - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data # named volume = data survives - ./initdb:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d:ro healthcheck: test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U ${POSTGRES_USER} -d n8n"] interval: 10s timeout: 5s retries: 5 networks: [backend] # NOT exposed to the host deploy: resources: limits: { memory: 1g } redis: image: redis:7-alpine restart: unless-stopped command: ["redis-server", "--appendonly", "yes", "--maxmemory", "256mb", "--maxmemory-policy", "allkeys-lru"] volumes: [redis_data:/data] healthcheck: test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"] interval: 10s retries: 5 networks: [backend] n8n-main: <<: *n8n-shared environment: <<: *n8n-env N8N_HOST: ${N8N_HOST} WEBHOOK_URL: https://${N8N_HOST}/ EXECUTIONS_DATA_PRUNE: "true" EXECUTIONS_DATA_MAX_AGE: "168" volumes: [n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n] networks: [backend, frontend] n8n-worker: <<: *n8n-shared command: worker --concurrency=10 deploy: replicas: 2 api: build: context: . dockerfile: Dockerfile target: runtime restart: unless-stopped environment: DATABASE_URL: postgresql://${POSTGRES_USER}:${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}@postgres:5432/n8n REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379/2 OPENAI_API_KEY: ${OPENAI_API_KEY} LOG_LEVEL: info depends_on: postgres: { condition: service_healthy } healthcheck: test: ["CMD", "curl", "-fsS", "http://localhost:8000/healthz"] interval: 30s start_period: 20s logging: driver: json-file options: { max-size: "10m", max-file: "3" } # prevents disk-filling logs networks: [backend, frontend] caddy: image: caddy:2-alpine restart: unless-stopped ports: ["80:80", "443:443"] # ONLY service exposed publicly volumes: - ./Caddyfile:/etc/caddy/Caddyfile:ro - caddy_data:/data networks: [frontend] networks: frontend: backend: internal: true # no outbound route from backend volumes: postgres_data: {} redis_data: {} n8n_data: {} caddy_data: {} ``` Several production details are load-bearing here. **Named volumes** (`postgres_data:`) are managed by Docker and survive `docker compose down`. Bind mounts (`./data:/var/lib/postgresql/data`) tie you to host paths and permissions. Use named volumes for databases, bind mounts for read-only config. **`depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy`** waits for the healthcheck to pass, not merely for the container to start. Without the condition, your API starts before Postgres accepts connections and crash-loops. **Two networks** mean Postgres and Redis are unreachable from the host and the internet — only Caddy publishes ports. This single arrangement eliminates a large class of exposure incidents. **Log rotation** matters more than people expect: an unbounded `json-file` driver will fill a disk and take the host down. ##### Secrets The layered approach, weakest to strongest: **A gitignored `.env` file** read by Compose via `${VAR}`. Adequate for development. Note that values set in `environment:` are visible in `docker inspect` and to anyone with Docker socket access. **Docker secrets** mount values as files at `/run/secrets/`, keeping them out of the environment and out of `inspect` output: ```yaml services: api: secrets: [openai_key] environment: OPENAI_API_KEY_FILE: /run/secrets/openai_key # app reads the file secrets: openai_key: file: ./secrets/openai_key.txt ``` **An external secret manager** (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Doppler) injected at startup is the right answer once you have more than one environment. Never bake secrets into an image with `ENV` or `ARG` — they persist in the layer history and travel with every copy of the image. ##### Operating the stack ```bash docker compose up -d --build # build and start docker compose ps # status + health docker compose logs -f api n8n-worker # follow specific services docker compose exec api bash # shell into a running container docker compose up -d --scale n8n-worker=4 docker compose pull && docker compose up -d # upgrade to new images docker compose down # stop; NAMED VOLUMES SURVIVE docker compose down -v # stop and DELETE volumes — destroys data docker system prune -af --volumes # reclaim disk (careful) docker image ls --format '{{.Repository}}:{{.Tag}}\t{{.Size}}' # measure sizes ``` ```mermaid flowchart TD I[Internet] -->|443| C[Caddy
TLS termination] subgraph frontend C --> M[n8n-main
UI + API] C --> A[FastAPI service] end subgraph backend["backend network — internal: true"] M --> P[(postgres
named volume)] M --> R[(redis
named volume)] A --> P A --> R W1[n8n-worker 1] --> R W2[n8n-worker 2] --> R W1 --> P W2 --> P end ``` ##### Common pitfalls - **`COPY . .` before installing dependencies**, destroying the layer cache. - **No `.dockerignore`**, shipping `.git` and `.venv` into the image. - **Running as root.** - **No named volume** on a database — data vanishes on recreate. - **`docker compose down -v` in production.** - **`latest` image tags**, causing unreproducible and surprising upgrades. - **`depends_on` without a health condition**, producing startup crash loops. - **Publishing database ports** to the host unnecessarily. - **Secrets in `ENV` or baked into layers.** - **No log rotation**, filling the disk. - **No resource limits**, letting one container starve the host. - **Assuming `localhost` works between services** — inside Compose, use the service name (`postgres`, `redis`). ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: write a `docker-compose.yml` running **n8n in queue mode, PostgreSQL, Redis and your FastAPI service** with **persistent volumes and healthchecks**, then **multi-stage build** the API image. Verify persistence properly — create an n8n workflow, run `docker compose down`, then `up -d`, and confirm the workflow is still there. If it is gone, your volume configuration is wrong, and finding that out locally is far better than in production. The mini project is that same stack made complete: internal-only backend network, Caddy in front with TLS, log rotation, resource limits, and a `.env.example` documenting every variable. Then hand the repository to someone else and see whether `docker compose up -d` gets them a working stack. Reproducibility is the actual deliverable. For the assignment, **convert your FastAPI image to a multi-stage, non-root build and measure the size reduction**. Record both numbers with `docker image ls`, and also time a code-only rebuild before and after moving the dependency install ahead of the source copy. Reporting "1.9 GB → 180 MB, and code-only rebuilds from 4 minutes to 20 seconds" is a far stronger result than image size alone, because build-cache behaviour is what you actually feel every day. ##### Key takeaways - Order Dockerfile instructions least-changing first, and copy dependencies before source — layer caching is the difference between 20-second and 4-minute rebuilds. - Multi-stage builds leave compilers and build tooling behind, and slim base images plus a `.dockerignore` typically cut size by an order of magnitude. - Always run as a non-root numeric UID and add a `HEALTHCHECK` so orchestrators know when the container is genuinely ready. - Use named volumes for stateful services, `depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy`, an internal backend network, log rotation and resource limits. - Keep secrets out of images and out of `ENV` where you can; version-pin every image tag so a stack is reproducible rather than merely runnable today.
